title: Your first home in Germany:

title: Why start now?
body: That's €1,500 rent a month for 10 years – paid to your landlord.
The same €1,500 can be the monthly EMI on a €300,000 loan.
foot: Example: 3.9% fixed for 10 years + 2% repayment (Dr. Klein best rate, 15.11.2026). Not a guarantee.

title: Know your budget
body: Rule of thumb: keep your EMI at about 35% of your net income.
Example: €4,300 net a month = around €1,500 EMI.
foot: Rule of thumb, not a bank decision. Banks check your full situation.

title: Save the buying costs
body: - Property transfer tax: 3.5% (Bavaria) to 6.5% (e.g. NRW)
- Notary + land registry: about 2%
- Agent: up to 3.57%
€400k flat = about €36k–48k on top. Many banks want this from your savings.
foot: Tax rates by state as of 2026.

title: Get your papers ready
body: - Passport + residence permit (e.g. Blue Card)
- Last 3–6 payslips + work contract
- Probation finished
- SCHUFA report
- Loans and EMIs in India – banks ask about them too

title: Compare banks
body: Not every German bank lends to expats – and conditions differ a lot.
A licensed broker compares many banks for you. A Blue Card can be enough.

title: Get a financing letter before you bid
body: Sellers and agents take you seriously when you can show the bank says yes in principle.

title: Notary: read the draft
body: The contract is in German. You usually get the draft 14 days before signing.
You can bring a translator. Ask every question before you sign.

title: Check state loans first
body: Families buying an older home can get the KfW loan "Jung kauft Alt" (up to €180,000).
Apply BEFORE you buy – not after.
foot: KfW programme 308, leaflet 08/2026. Rules can change.
